**(B)** Dendron

Dendrons are the short, branched processes of the cyton that receive signals and transmit the message towards the cell body. The axon carries messages away from the cyton, the nodes of Ranvier are gaps in the myelin sheath where the impulse jumps during saltatory conduction, and the neurilemma is the outer covering of the nerve fibre.

**(C)** Acetyl choline

Acetylcholine is released at the terminal ends of nerve fibres, for example by postganglionic parasympathetic (cholinergic) fibres, and is destroyed by cholinesterase after the impulse crosses the synapse. ADH is a hormone acting on the kidney, acetyl CoA is a metabolic intermediate, and inositol is part of a second messenger (inositol triphosphate), not a neurotransmitter.

**(D)** Schwann cells

Schwann cells are the most abundant glial cells of the PNS and produce the myelin sheath around medullated peripheral nerves. Oligodendrocytes form myelin in the CNS, satellite cells only support peripheral neurons, and astrocytes are CNS cells that maintain the blood-brain barrier.

**(D)** Ganglion

A ganglion is a cluster of neuron cell bodies lying outside the CNS, such as the dorsal root ganglion beside the spinal cord, which holds the cell bodies of sensory neurons. A nucleus is a group of cell bodies inside the CNS, a tract is a bundle of axons inside the CNS, and a nerve is a bundle of axons outside it.

[Note: the chapter places cytons in the ganglia and names the dorsal root ganglion but does not define a ganglion in these words; standard biology gives this definition.]

**(B)** on cell surface

Protein and peptide hormones are not lipid soluble, so they cannot cross the plasma membrane; they bind to receptors on the cell surface and act through a second messenger such as cAMP. Only lipid-soluble steroid and thyroid hormones enter the cell and bind receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus.

**(B)** disturbance of \(\text{Ca}^{++}\)

Parathormone raises blood calcium by drawing calcium from bones, increasing its absorption in the gut and reducing its loss in urine. Without the parathyroids, blood calcium falls, nerves and muscles become over-excitable and parathyroid (hypocalcaemic) tetany follows. Myxoedema is a thyroxine deficiency in adults, and ageing and raised blood pressure are not the specific results of losing these glands.

**(D)** Tyrosine

Thyroxine is made by attaching iodine to the amino acid tyrosine, and adrenaline and noradrenaline are catecholamines also derived from tyrosine in the adrenal medulla. Glycine, arginine and ornithine are not the precursors of these hormones.

[Note: the chapter states that thyroxine is made from tyrosine but not that adrenaline and noradrenaline are; standard biology gives tyrosine as the precursor of the catecholamines too.]

**(D)** behaviour

Pheromones are volatile chemicals released by an organism that produce a response in other members of the same species, and signalling pheromones in particular induce behavioural responses such as mating, locating food or warning of danger in ants. They do not act on the skin colour, excretion or digestion of the animal that smells them.

**(C)** Pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, thymus

All four of these are separate, purely endocrine (ductless) glands. The other sets each contain an organ that is not a discrete endocrine gland: salivary glands are exocrine, the liver is mainly an exocrine and metabolic organ, and the pancreas is both exocrine and endocrine, with its endocrine part only scattered islets of Langerhans.

[Note: the chapter does not use the term "discrete endocrine gland"; standard biology uses it for glands that are wholly endocrine.]

**(A)** Corpus luteum

After ovulation, LH induces the ruptured Graafian follicle to develop into the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone. The corpus albicans is the scar that forms later when the corpus luteum degenerates, the corpus spongiosum is erectile tissue of the penis, and the corpus callosum joins the two cerebral hemispheres.

**(C)** Insulin - Hyperglycemia

Reduced insulin secretion by the beta cells raises the blood glucose level, giving diabetes mellitus (hyperglycemia). The other pairs are mismatched: diabetes insipidus comes from a deficiency of ADH, not parathyroid hormone; LH deficiency does not cause diabetes mellitus; and tetany comes from a deficiency of parathormone, not thyroxine.

**(D)** Piamater

The pia mater is the innermost, delicate and highly vascular meninx that lies in close contact with the brain and spinal cord. The dura mater is the outermost meninx attached to the cranium, the arachnoid lies between the two, and the cranium is the bony case outside all three meninges.
